 Proteus] A sea-god with the power to change shape, and to foretell the future (see Virgil, Georgic iv
387ff.). S.’s conception of Proteus, as the informing spirit of the natural human world, appears particu-
larly indebted to Bacon (a favourite of S.’s); cp. TL 269–73, Prose Works 250 and see Wasserman 348–9.
 Murray’s ed. note in Prose Works 465 explains that S. thinks of Proteus ‘not as the prophetic old man
of the sea but, in the Orphic mystical sense, as the source of the elemental material world, a symbolic
application of his character derived from his ability to change into whatever shape he pleased until
caught in one of them, on which occasion he was obliged to truthfully answer any query put to him.’
